own_scenes.family: Los pioneros: Atkins, May, Saunderson y la primera ola
own_scenes.desc: El más joven de los tres de Belleville, nacido en Brooklyn en 1964, se hizo amigo de May en el equipo de fútbol americano del instituto (de un puñetazo). Mientras estudiaba en la Eastern Michigan University vio pinchar a Eddie Fowlkes, entró en Deep Space y en el Street Beat de May, donde aprendió a reeditar discos ajenos. En el sótano de May creó en 1985 KMS (Kevin Maurice Saunderson) y, con Santonio Echols, algunos de los temas más brutales del techno de los ochenta, pero también quiso hacer discos «de verdad» con voz («Triangle of Love»). «Big Fun», con ritmo de James «Jit» Pennington y melodía de Art Forrest (pagados a tarifa de músico), encontró su voz en la cantante de house de Chicago Paris Grey, por consejo de Terry «Housemaster» Baldwin. Como Inner City (con Roy Holmon, luego Dennis White, Tommy Onyx y el DJ Darrell «D» Wynn), el álbum Big Fun (1989) dio cuatro números uno de la lista de baile de Billboard; ocho veces en el Top 40 británico y casi seis millones de discos: el mayor éxito comercial del techno de los ochenta.

notes.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995
notes.text: Tras el fracaso del R&B de Fire (1990), Inner City volvió a lo básico y a la espiritualidad del gospel en Praise (1992), con «Let It Reign» y «Hallelujah» cantadas por Paris Grey como en la iglesia y la colaboración de Altern 8 (Chris Peat y Mark Archer, alias Nexus 21): himnos de Detroit con pianos y breakbeats.

refs.q: Street Beat was different because it wasn’t just mixing, but edits, using the pause button, creating wild sounds, and all that. You’d basically do a whole new production . . . getting creative with someone else’s record. I took that concept from Derrick.
refs.para: Before Derrick’s [May’s] show, I was playing football for Eastern Michigan. I eventually decided that was it: I wasn’t going to make it to the pros at that school, so I took another angle and started [DJing]. After I saw Eddie Fowlkes spin at a fraternity party, I jumped into the clique [Deep Space] and started practicing my ass off. Street Beat was different because it wasn’t just mixing, but edits, using the pause button, creating wild sounds, and all that. You’d basically do a whole new production . . . getting creative with someone else’s record. I took that concept from Derrick.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: Time to Express: Techno’s First Artists Emerge, 1981–1989

refs.q: “Kevin had a knack for pulling the right people together to get the job done,” says Payne, by this time working promotions for KMS. “He was real good at that.”
refs.para: Hitting the U.K. Top 40 eight times and selling close to six million records, Inner City would go on to become one of techno’s greatest market successes of the 1980s, largely due to the talents and vision of Kevin Saunderson. “Kevin had a knack for pulling the right people together to get the job done,” says Payne, by this time working promotions for KMS. “He was real good at that.”
